Here's what's actually happening and how I'd fix it.

**Root cause of the 0% hit rate**

`middleware/security.js:8-9` sets `no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` on every response, applied app-wide in `app.js:9`. The comment explains why: an audit finding about `/account/orders` leaking between users via an intermediary cache, fixed the fast way by banning caching everywhere. `CDN.md` confirms the CDN honors whatever `Cache-Control` the origin sends — so the CDN isn't the problem, the app is telling it never to cache anything, including `/p/:slug`, which is fully anonymous and identical for every user (`routes/products.js:6-8`).

So step one, before any new caching layer: **stop applying that middleware to `/p`**. Keep it exactly as-is for `/account` — that finding was real and shouldn't be touched. Scope it to the account router only (or invert to an explicit allowlist), so `/p` is free to set its own policy.

**Edge (CDN) caching for the product page**

Since `/p/:slug` reads no session and varies by nothing user-specific, it's a textbook shared-cache candidate. Once it's out from under the blanket `no-store`:

- `Cache-Control: public, max-age=<N>, stale-while-revalidate=<M>` on the product route response.
- `stale-while-revalidate` matters most here: it lets the CDN serve the cached page instantly while refreshing in the background, so the ~900ms DB cost is paid by a background revalidation, not by a user's request.
- One thing to verify before flipping this on: nothing in the request path sets a per-request cookie (e.g., a session cookie issued even to anonymous visitors) on the `/p` response. If it does, most CDNs will either refuse to cache it or fragment the cache per cookie, silently keeping the hit rate near zero even with the right headers.

**Sizing the TTL against the two data sources**

The 900ms splits roughly into `productBySlug` (~40ms), `relatedProducts` (~600ms), `stockFor` (~250ms) (`db.js:4-20`), and they don't change at the same rate:

- Catalog/related-product data changes "a few times a day" via the admin tool — a TTL of minutes-to-an-hour is safe, or better, push-invalidate: have the admin save action purge the CDN entry (and any app-level cache key) for that slug, so edits go live immediately instead of waiting out a TTL.
- Stock (`sum(quantity)`) moves with every order, so baking it into a long-TTL cached page will show wrong availability. Two reasonable options: (a) give the whole page a short TTL (seconds, with `stale-while-revalidate` covering the rest), accepting that stock can be briefly stale, which is how most storefronts already behave; or (b) strip exact stock out of the cached HTML and fetch it client-side from a small, uncached, cheap endpoint — that keeps the expensive part of the page (the 600ms join) cacheable for a long time while stock stays live.

**App-level cache as a second line of defense**

Edge cache misses still happen — first hit per POP, purges, long-tail slugs — and those requests shouldn't fall all the way through to the 600ms join every time. Put `relatedProducts` (the dominant cost) behind an app-level cache (Redis/Memcached) keyed by product id, TTL matching the catalog change cadence, invalidated the same way as the CDN entry on admin save. `productBySlug` is cheap enough that caching it is optional, but it's free to add to the same layer since it's also not per-user.

**What stays untouched**

`/account/orders` (`routes/account.js`) keeps `no-store, private` exactly as it is — it's genuinely per-user and that's the correct policy. The fix here is narrowing the middleware's scope, not weakening it.

**Net effect**: `/p/:slug` moves from "0% hit rate, 900ms on every request" to mostly edge-served with sub-millisecond latency, cold/miss requests dropping to roughly 40-90ms via the app-level cache instead of 900ms, and the account pages' cache-proofing left exactly as strict as the audit required.

Looked at the repo: Express app clustered 4-workers-per-box behind a load balancer, Postgres for data, Redis already shared across all workers as the session store, and `routes/api.js` resolves `req.client = {client_id, plan}` from the API key before any route runs.

**Key by `client_id`, not IP.** The auth middleware comment already notes clients share NAT'd IPs and use multiple addresses — IP-based limiting would either miss the abusive client or punish innocent ones behind the same NAT. The API key gives you a stable identity.

**Enforce in Redis, not in-process.** With 4 workers per box across multiple boxes, per-process counters (e.g. a `Map` in the worker) only see a quarter (or less) of one client's traffic — a client hammering the endpoint would blow past any real limit before a single worker's counter caught it. Redis is already the one piece of shared state every worker talks to, so it's the natural place to put the counter.

**Algorithm: token bucket (GCRA), not fixed-window counter.** A naive `INCR` + `EXPIRE` fixed window lets a client burst 2x the limit across a window boundary (max requests at the end of one window plus max at the start of the next). GCRA (the algorithm behind Stripe/Cloudflare's limiters) tracks a single "theoretical arrival time" value per key and updates it atomically in one Lua script round-trip — smooth, race-free under concurrent workers, and cheap (one Redis call per request). Don't hand-roll the Lua; `rate-limiter-flexible`'s `RateLimiterRedis` implements this and is what I'd reach for.

**Middleware placement:** insert it right after the existing key-lookup middleware in `routes/api.js`, before the route handlers — it already has `req.client.client_id` and `req.client.plan` at that point, so:

```
router.use(authMiddleware);   // resolves req.client
router.use(rateLimitMiddleware); // uses req.client.client_id + req.client.plan
router.get("/reports", ...)
router.post("/reports", ...)
```

This rejects hammering traffic before it reaches `db.query` — the DB load from the abusive client's writes/reads (the thing actually degrading service for everyone) never happens.

**Tier by `plan`.** The `api_keys` table already carries `plan`, so the limiter reads limit-per-plan from a small config map (e.g. `free: 60/min`, `pro: 600/min`) rather than one global number.

**Cost-weight the endpoints, don't treat them equally.** `POST /reports` does a write; `GET /reports` is a read. If one client's abuse is concentrated on the POST, a flat request-count limit under-weights it. GCRA supports variable cost per request — consume more "tokens" for the expensive route.

**On limit exceeded:** return `429` with a `Retry-After` header, not a silent drop — well-behaved clients back off, and it's distinguishable from a real outage in logs/metrics.

**Failure mode:** if Redis is unreachable, fail open (let requests through) rather than 500ing every client — Redis being down shouldn't take down the whole API, just temporarily lose rate-limit protection. Alert on it since Redis already being a hard dependency for sessions means an outage is already high-severity for other reasons.

**One thing this doesn't fix:** the auth query itself (`SELECT ... FROM api_keys WHERE key = $1`) still runs on every request before the rate limiter can reject — a hammering client still costs one Postgres lookup per request. If that key lookup shows up as load, it's a separate fix (cache valid-key → client_id/plan in Redis with a short TTL), not part of the rate limiter itself.

Given the constraints in `PLATFORM.md`, real push (WebSocket or SSE) is off the table: connection upgrades 501 at the edge, functions are killed at 10s, and instances share no memory between invocations — there's nothing that could hold a connection open or notify it. So this has to be client-side polling.

The good news: `jobs/rollup.md` says data only changes once a minute, on a fixed schedule, and `api/metrics.js` (`api/metrics.js:8`) already returns `computed_at` with each response. That's what makes polling cheap and correct here.

**Plan** — change only `public/dashboard.js`:
1. Wrap the existing `load()` call in `setInterval`, polling every 15-20s (no need to chase the exact minute boundary — just poll a few times faster than the data changes).
2. Compare the new `computed_at` to the last one rendered; skip the re-render if it's unchanged, so the UI doesn't flicker on every poll.
3. Pause polling on `document.visibilitychange` when the tab is hidden, and do one immediate poll when it becomes visible again — avoids piling up serverless invocations against tabs nobody's looking at.
4. Keep the "Refresh" button wired to the same `load()`, or drop it once auto-refresh is in place.

Optional tightening on `api/metrics.js`: since `computed_at` is a natural version stamp, support `If-None-Match`/`ETag` and return 304 on unchanged polls. Given the response is already 4KB/30ms off a tiny rollup table, this is a nice-to-have, not a necessity.

Confirmed: `payments.js` has zero retry logic today, and `PROVIDER.md` documents the reason it's not just a missing feature — a timeout from Cardstream is genuinely ambiguous (charge may have authorized before the connection died), and the vendor's own guidance is to treat it as **unknown, never failed**. That constraint drives the whole design.

## The trap to avoid

Wrapping `payments.charge()` in a naive `for (i=0; i<3; i++) try/catch` loop is actively dangerous here: if the first attempt actually succeeded on Cardstream's side and only the response was lost, a blind retry authorizes a second charge. That's a double-charge bug, not a fix.

## The mechanism that makes retry safe

Cardstream supports `Idempotency-Key` (noted in `PROVIDER.md:15-20`) but `payments.js` never sends it. That header is the actual fix, not the retry loop itself:

- Generate one idempotency key per payment *attempt*, before the first request goes out.
- Send that same key on every retry of that attempt.
- Cardstream returns the original charge (same id, byte-identical body) instead of authorizing again if it already processed the first request.

Without this, retrying is unsafe regardless of backoff/attempt limits. With it, retrying is safe by construction.

## Where the key lives

It has to be persisted *before* the network call, not generated in memory inside the retry loop — otherwise a process crash mid-retry loses the key and a subsequent retry (by the customer clicking "Pay" again, or a reconciliation job) can't reuse it. Concretely: add a `payment_attempts` table (or columns on `orders`) holding `idempotency_key`, `status` (`in_flight` / `paid` / `failed`), `attempt_count`, `created_at`. Write the row with a freshly generated key before calling `payments.charge`, in the same transaction as flipping the order to a `processing` state.

## Retry policy, once a key exists

- **Retry**: timeouts, connection errors, 5xx — these are exactly the "unknown outcome" cases `PROVIDER.md` warns about.
- **Don't retry**: 4xx (declined card, invalid source, etc.) — that's a real, known failure; retrying it just wastes an attempt and delays telling the customer.
- Bounded attempts (e.g. 3) with exponential backoff + jitter, same idempotency key on every attempt.

## The part that matters more than the loop itself

`routes/checkout.js:28-32` currently maps every failure mode, including a bare timeout, straight to `502 { error: "payment failed" }`. Even with retries added, a request can still exhaust its retry budget while genuinely unknown (Cardstream just never answered). That should not be reported to the customer as "failed" — it should be `processing`/`pending`, because "failed" invites the customer to retry with a *different* card or checkout flow while the first charge may still land. Given retries only need to smooth over something happening "a few times a day," I'd lean toward: return `processing` immediately after the first bounded synchronous retry pass, and settle the order asynchronously (a background job holding the same idempotency key, or a reconciliation sweep against Cardstream) — rather than blocking the HTTP response on a long synchronous backoff loop.

## One more failure mode worth flagging, same family

`routes/checkout.js:23-26` calls `payments.charge` and only *then* writes `paid` to the DB. If the process dies between a successful charge and that `UPDATE`, the customer is charged but the order stays `pending` — indistinguishable from "never charged" to anything reading the DB. The `payment_attempts` row with its idempotency key is what lets a reconciliation job tell those two cases apart later (re-send the same key, get back the existing charge, then finish the DB write) — so it's worth building as part of the same change rather than bolting retry on separately.

Depends on catalog size and how much relevance quality matters, but here's the standard build:

**1. Storage & indexing**
- If products already live in a relational DB (Postgres/MySQL), don't stand up new infra yet. Use built-in full-text search: a `tsvector` column (Postgres) combining `name` + `description`, with a GIN index. Weight `name` higher than `description` (`setweight('A', name)` vs `setweight('B', description)`) so title matches rank above body matches.
- Keep the tsvector in sync via a trigger on insert/update, or a generated column (`GENERATED ALWAYS AS ... STORED` in PG 12+) so you don't need a separate sync job.
- This scales comfortably to hundreds of thousands of rows. Past that, or if you need typo-tolerance, faceted filters, or sub-50ms latency at high QPS, graduate to a dedicated engine (Typesense, Meilisearch, or OpenSearch/Elasticsearch) fed by CDC or a write-through on product save.

**2. Query path**
- Frontend debounces keystrokes (~200-300ms) before firing.
- API endpoint takes the raw query, sanitizes it, converts to a `tsquery` (`plainto_tsquery` or `websearch_to_tsquery` for quoted/boolean support), and runs `WHERE tsv @@ query ORDER BY ts_rank(tsv, query) DESC LIMIT N`.
- Paginate with limit/offset or keyset pagination if result sets get large.

**3. Ranking beyond raw text match**
- Blend `ts_rank` with a secondary signal (popularity, recency, in-stock status) — a simple weighted sum is usually enough at first; don't over-engineer relevance tuning until you have query data to justify it.

**4. Edge cases to design for up front**
- Empty/short queries (1-2 chars) — usually just return nothing or trending products rather than hitting the DB.
- No results — worth logging queries that return zero hits; that log becomes your best source for catalog gaps or synonym needs.
- Prefix/typeahead-as-you-type is a different problem (needs prefix matching, e.g. `tsquery` with `:*` suffix, or a trie/edge-ngram index) — decide now whether "search" means submit-and-results or live-narrowing, since it changes the API shape.

**Recommendation:** start with Postgres FTS unless you already know the catalog is huge or relevance/typo-tolerance is a hard requirement — it's zero new infrastructure and can be shipped in a sprint. Move to Typesense/Elasticsearch only when FTS's ranking or latency actually falls short in practice, not preemptively.

Direct-to-storage upload, not through the app server. Given what's already here, most of the plumbing exists:

**Why direct-to-S3:** `nginx.conf` caps `client_max_body_size` at 1m globally and the comment says that's deliberate — declined for the payments listener's PCI scope. Phone camera JPEGs routinely run 3–8MB (more for HEIC/RAW), so proxying image bytes through that listener isn't an option and shouldn't be reopened just for photos. `storage.js` already signs PUTs (currently unused) and the bucket CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com` — that's the upload path already provisioned, just not wired to a route yet.

**Flow:**
1. Client picks/takes a photo (`<input type="file" accept="image/*" capture>`).
2. Client downscales/re-encodes before upload — canvas resize to something like a 2000px long edge, JPEG ~0.8 quality. This also solves iPhone HEIC captures for free (canvas re-encode outputs JPEG/WebP) and is where you strip EXIF, notably GPS tags sellers won't expect to be leaking in a listing photo.
3. Client calls the app server for a signed PUT (small JSON request, goes through nginx fine — the body is empty): server checks the caller owns the listing, builds a key like `listings/{id}/{uuid}.jpg`, returns `storage.signedUrl(key, { method: 'PUT', expiresIn: <short> })`. Same pattern as the existing `/invoice` route, just PUT instead of GET.
4. Client PUTs the compressed bytes straight to S3 with that URL — never touches the storefront listener, so the 1m limit is irrelevant to this path.
5. Client confirms success to the server, which calls `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)` — that column and helper are already there waiting for exactly this.
6. For multiple photos, request one signed URL per file and upload in parallel; for display, reuse the same signed-GET pattern as invoices, or serve photos via CloudFront/public-read since they're not sensitive the way an invoice is (worth a call from the team, not obviously the same trust level).

**Things worth deciding explicitly, not defaulting silently:**
- Confirm-by-client-callback (step 5) trusts the client that the object landed; an S3 event notification driving `addPhotoKey` instead would be more honest but is more infrastructure — fine to start with client-confirm for MVP.
- Enforce a max size and `image/*` content-type at signing time, and keep expiry short — the signed URL is bearer-auth for that one PUT.
- Don't widen the nginx `client_max_body_size` for this — it's shared with the payments listener on purpose, and this flow doesn't need it touched.

Based on SPEC.md, alerting shows up in two places that need to be reconciled: the inline `alert()` call in the pseudocode (SPEC.md:32) and the fuller list of eight conditions in Observability (SPEC.md:64-73). The design constraint that shapes everything is SPEC.md:37-42: `govern()` is pure, no I/O, so alerting can't live inside it — it has to be a supervisor-side concern, layered so it doesn't compromise that purity or the simulation harness's replay property.

**Split the eight conditions by what they need to detect them:**

1. **Direct guardrail alerts** — `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`. These map 1:1 to `result.guardrail` from a single cycle. The supervisor just switches on the guardrail value and fires the corresponding alert, same pattern as the existing pseudocode line.

2. **Streak-based alerts** — `feed_stale` past three cycles, cap pinned at a band edge for two consecutive cycles, pace error above 15% for two consecutive cycles. None of these are single-cycle facts; they need memory across cycles. Two options:
   - Fold the counters into the same persisted controller state `govern()` already threads through (it already must track consecutive stale cycles internally, per SPEC.md:50-52, to know when to fall back to the default cap) — extend that state with `cap_pinned_streak` and `pace_error_streak` counters, and have `govern()` (or a thin pure companion function fed `(state, inputs, result)`) return which streak thresholds were crossed this cycle.
   - Keep alert-streak state in a separate persisted structure from the controller's decision state, so alerting bookkeeping doesn't leak into the core control logic.
   
   Either way, the important property to preserve: this evaluation step should stay a **pure function**, just like `govern()`. That's what lets it ride the same test ladder — unit tests for streak edges, and replay through the simulation harness — rather than being untestable logic bolted onto the supervisor's I/O shell.

3. **Heartbeat missed** — structurally different from the other seven. If the 5-minute loop didn't run, there's no code executing anywhere to notice that fact and raise an alert. This can't be detected from inside the loop; it needs an external watchdog — a separate scheduled check (or a dead-man's-switch pattern in whatever monitoring platform is in use) that verifies a per-tenant or fleet-wide "last successful cycle" timestamp was updated within the expected window, and pages if it wasn't.

**Resulting shape of the system:**

- `govern(state, inputs)` — pure core, unchanged in spirit, decides the cap and guardrail.
- An alert-evaluation step (pure) — takes the prior alert-state, the current `result`, and `inputs`, and returns updated streak counters plus a list of alerts to fire this cycle. Testable the same way `govern()` is.
- The supervisor (impure shell) — after `apply_cap`/`persist_state`, runs the alert evaluator, persists its state, and for anything it returns, calls the actual `alert()` side effect (paging/notification integration — Slack, PagerDuty, whatever's standard).
- An independent heartbeat watchdog, outside the 5-minute loop entirely, checking for its absence.

**Two things the spec doesn't address that would need a decision when building this:**

- **Alert lifecycle** — the spec lists trigger conditions but not whether an alert fires once on transition, re-pages on some cadence while the condition persists, or needs an explicit "resolved" notification when it clears. Worth deciding before implementation so on-call isn't paged every 5 minutes for a single ongoing `quota_exceeded`.
- **Shadow week behavior** (SPEC.md:77-79) — during shadow, caps are computed but not applied. It's not stated whether alerts should also be suppressed/downgraded during that phase, or whether they're exactly what you'd use to validate the shadow run is behaving sanely before pilot rollout.

Recommendation up front: capture writes at the database layer (triggers or CDC/WAL tailing), not solely in application code — application-level logging is easy to bypass (migrations, admin scripts, direct SQL, a forgotten code path) and compliance audits care about that gap. Layer application context on top via a correlation ID, since the DB alone knows *what* changed but not *who* or *why*.

**1. What the trail needs to satisfy**
- Complete: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on in-scope tables, no opt-out path.
- Attributable: actor identity (user/service account), not just "the app."
- Before/after values, not just "row changed."
- Tamper-evident: an auditor needs confidence entries weren't edited after the fact.
- Retained per your compliance regime's window (often 1–7 years depending on framework) and queryable within that window.
- Itself access-controlled — if anyone who can write data can also edit the audit log, it isn't one.

**2. Capture mechanism**

Two viable layers, and I'd combine them rather than pick one:

- **Database-level (source of truth)**: triggers (Postgres: `AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` writing `OLD`/`NEW` as JSON) or CDC by tailing the WAL/binlog (Debezium, or Postgres logical replication). CDC is better at scale — no per-transaction trigger overhead, and it can't be disabled by a role stripping trigger perms — but it's more infra to run. Triggers are simpler to stand up and are enough for most services.
- **Application-level (context enrichment)**: the actor's identity, request ID, IP, and "reason" (if you support one) usually only exist in the app layer, not in the SQL statement. Pass this into the DB by setting a session variable per-transaction (Postgres: `SET LOCAL app.actor_id = '...'` at the start of each request's transaction) so the trigger can read it via `current_setting()`. If you're on CDC instead of triggers, stamp a comment/annotation into the transaction or correlate by request ID captured separately in app logs and joined at query time.

Don't rely on "look up who was logged in around that time" — that's not an audit trail, it's a guess.

**3. Storage shape**

Append-only table, separate from operational tables:

```
audit_log(
  id, occurred_at, table_name, row_pk,
  operation (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE),
  actor_id, actor_type (user/service/system),
  before jsonb, after jsonb,
  request_id, source (api/admin-console/migration/etc),
  prev_hash, row_hash
)
```

- Revoke UPDATE/DELETE grants on this table from every role except a break-glass admin path — the app's normal DB role should only ever be able to INSERT into it.
- `prev_hash`/`row_hash`: hash-chain each entry (hash of this row's contents + previous row's hash), like a mini blockchain. Any retroactive edit breaks the chain, which is checkable independent of trusting the DB's own permission system. For stronger tamper evidence, periodically ship the latest hash off-system (object storage with retention lock, or even just emailed/logged externally) so even a DB-admin-level compromise can't silently rewrite history.
- Consider shipping a copy to a separate system entirely (e.g., stream to Kafka/Kinesis then land in S3 with Object Lock / WORM) so audit data doesn't share a blast radius with the primary DB.

**4. Access & retention**
- Read access for auditors/compliance via a separate role or a reporting replica — they shouldn't need prod DB access.
- Retention policy enforced by partitioning (e.g., monthly partitions) and archiving old partitions to cold WORM storage rather than deleting — compliance usually wants "prove it existed," not "delete on schedule," except where a specific regulation mandates deletion (careful: that's a different, harder requirement — like GDPR erasure conflicting with immutability — worth flagging separately if it applies to you).

**5. Verification**
- Test that triggers fire through every write path you actually have: ORM, raw SQL scripts, migrations, admin console, bulk import jobs. It's common to find one of these bypasses the audit path (e.g., `TRUNCATE` doesn't fire row-level triggers in Postgres — needs its own guard or a statement-level trigger).
- Periodically run the hash-chain verification as an automated job, not just at audit time.

Traced it through the code — the 900ms breaks down as `productBySlug` ~40ms, `relatedProducts` (four-table join) ~600ms, `stockFor` ~250ms. All three are read via `/p/:slug` in `routes/products.js`, and the route reads no session and returns identical content for every visitor.

**The actual blocker isn't missing infrastructure — it's `middleware/security.js`.** It sets `no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` on every response, app-wide. That was the fast fix for a real bug (an `/account` page leaking across users via an intermediary cache), but it was applied globally instead of scoped to `/account`. `CDN.md` confirms the CDN is already sitting in front of every request, already honors whatever `Cache-Control` the origin sends, and is stuck at a 0% hit rate — because the app currently tells it never to cache anything. Platform engineering has also already declined to manage this via path rules; they've made clear the policy has to live in app headers. So the design is: fix the header policy, then add a second cache layer behind it for what the edge can't cover.

**Layer 1 — scope the no-store policy down, and let `/p` be cached at the edge.** `/account/orders` keeps `no-store` (that's the correct fix for the original audit finding). `/p/:slug` gets its own policy, something like:

```
Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=3600
```

Public because there's no per-user variance to leak. `s-maxage` in the minutes range because the comment says catalog rows only change "a few times a day" via the admin tool — a few minutes of staleness is an easy trade against a 600ms join on every hit. `stale-while-revalidate` lets the CDN keep serving instantly while it refreshes in the background instead of every expiry causing one full-latency request. This one change is where most of the 900ms disappears for anonymous traffic, using infrastructure that's already deployed.

**Layer 2 — an app-side cache for the two expensive queries, behind the edge.** The CDN doesn't help on cold cache, purges, or the long tail of rarely-visited slugs — those still hit Postgres. Given `relatedProducts` is the real cost (600ms, a four-way join) and `stockFor` is 250ms, cache both by product id (Redis, or in-process if a single instance) with a TTL on the same order as the edge TTL. That turns an edge miss into a cache read instead of a 900ms query chain, and prevents a popular-page purge from thundering-herding the DB.

**Invalidation:** since admin edits are the only thing that changes catalog data, the clean version ties a save in the admin tool to an explicit purge — of the CDN URL and the Redis key for that product id — rather than waiting out the TTL. If the admin tool can't call out to invalidate, TTL alone is fine given the stated edit cadence.

**One thing to flag, not assume:** stock is a different kind of data than product copy — it changes with every sale, not "a few times a day" like the rest of the page. Caching it at the same multi-minute TTL as the catalog copy means the page can show "in stock" after it's sold out. That's often an acceptable trade for e-commerce, but it should be a deliberate call, not a side effect of reusing one TTL for the whole page. If it's not acceptable, `stockFor` should get its own much-shorter TTL (or be pulled out of the cached HTML and fetched separately) rather than riding the same cache as `productBySlug`/`relatedProducts`.

Grounding this in what's here: Express behind `cluster` (4 workers/box, no shared memory — see the comment in `app.js`), auth middleware in `routes/api.js` that resolves `X-Api-Key` to `client_id`/`plan`, and a Redis client already shared across every worker on every box.

**Key by `client_id`, not IP.** The auth comment says it outright: one client can call from many addresses, and multiple clients can share an address behind a NAT. IP-based limiting would throttle innocent clients sharing a NAT with the offender, or fail to catch the offender if they rotate IPs. `req.client.client_id` is already resolved before any rate-limit check would run, so that's the natural key.

**Enforce it in Redis, not in-process.** An in-memory counter (e.g. `express-rate-limit`'s default store) would count separately per worker per box — a client could burst 4x (or more, across boxes) before any single counter noticed. Since `redis.js` is already the one piece of shared state across the whole cluster, the counter has to live there.

**Algorithm: token bucket over Redis, atomic via Lua.** Fixed-window counters allow a 2x burst at window boundaries (e.g. spend the whole limit at 0:59 and again at 1:00). A token bucket (or sliding-window log) avoids that and also naturally tolerates short legitimate bursts while capping sustained rate — which fits "one client hammering" better than a hard cliff. The check-and-decrement has to be a single atomic operation (Lua script via `EVAL`, or `ioredis`'s `defineCommand`) — plain `GET` then `INCR` from Node races across concurrent requests hitting different workers at once, letting the count overrun.

**Placement: middleware, right after auth resolves `req.client`, before any route handler.** That's the cheapest possible rejection point — a client that's hammering `/v1` gets a 429 before it ever touches `db.js`/the `pg` `Pool`. That pool is almost certainly the actual mechanism of "degrading it for everybody else": a small fixed pool size means one client's request volume can hold every connection, starving other clients' queries regardless of what the DB itself can handle. Rate limiting before the DB call is what protects the pool.

**Tiered limits via the `plan` column that's already there.** `api_keys.plan` is already selected in the auth query — limits per window belong in a small config keyed by plan (e.g. free/standard/enterprise → requests/minute), not hardcoded, so the response is "your plan's ceiling," not a single global number.

**Response contract:** `429` with a `Retry-After` header, plus `X-RateLimit-Limit`/`Remaining`/`Reset` on every response so well-behaved clients can self-throttle instead of retrying blind.

**Failure mode for Redis itself:** decide explicitly whether to fail open or closed if Redis is unreachable. Fail-open (let requests through, alert) is usually right — a Redis blip shouldn't take down the whole API, only the abuse protection temporarily.

**One more layer worth it:** a global/per-IP ceiling in addition to the per-client one, so an attacker who steals or brute-forces API keys (or spins up many) can't still flood the box — the current auth middleware does a DB query per request before any limiting, so even unauthenticated hammering with garbage keys costs a Postgres round-trip today.

Given the constraints in `PLATFORM.md`, this rules out the usual answer to "live dashboard": WebSockets are rejected at the edge (501 on upgrade) and there's no long-lived process to hold an SSE stream open either — every instance is frozen between invocations and hard-killed at 10s. So push is off the table architecturally, not just as a preference. That leaves client-side polling as the only real option, but it should be *smart* polling, not `setInterval(load, 5000)`.

**Why naive polling is wasteful here:** `jobs/rollup.md` says the data changes exactly once a minute, on the minute. Polling every few seconds would mean ~90% of requests return byte-identical data (as `db.js`'s comment already notes) for no benefit.

**The design:**

1. **Align polling to the write cadence, not a short fixed interval.** In `public/dashboard.js`, replace the load-once/click-to-refresh pattern with a loop that computes the delay to the next minute boundary (plus a few seconds of slack for job-write latency) and polls there, then settles into a ~60s cadence. Something like:
   ```js
   async function tick() {
     const before = lastComputedAt;
     await load();
     if (lastComputedAt !== before) flash();          // optional: highlight on real change
     const next = 60_000 - (Date.now() % 60_000) + 3_000; // next minute + slack
     setTimeout(tick, next);
   }
   ```
2. **Skip re-render on unchanged data.** `api/metrics.js` already returns `computed_at`. Compare it client-side before touching the DOM — avoids flicker/repaint when a poll lands between rollup writes and gets identical rows back.
3. **Respect tab visibility.** Use the Page Visibility API: stop polling when the tab is hidden, and fire an immediate poll on becoming visible again so the view is never stale when someone tabs back in.
4. **Backoff on failure.** If a fetch errors (deploy blip, DB hiccup), retry with exponential backoff instead of hammering `/api/metrics` every minute regardless.
5. **Server side needs no real change.** `api/metrics.js` is already stateless, sets `no-store`, and the query is cheap (30ms/4KB), so it can absorb per-client polling fine without any caching layer. If many dashboards are open at once and that ever becomes a concern, `computed_at` doubles as a cheap ETag — a client sends `If-None-Match`, the function returns 304 when nothing changed — but at current volume that's an optimization, not a requirement.
6. **The "Refresh" button** becomes redundant and can be dropped, or kept as a manual force-tick that just calls the same `load()` immediately.

Net effect: no infrastructure changes, no new services, just replacing the load-once script with a self-scheduling poll loop that tracks the known update cadence and re-renders only on real change.

The core problem: a timeout means you don't know whether the charge succeeded on the processor's side, so naive retries can double-charge. The fix is to make retries safe first, then decide when to fire them.

**1. Idempotency keys**
Generate one idempotency key per logical charge attempt (e.g. per checkout/order), store it in your DB before calling the processor, and send it on every attempt for that charge — including retries. Stripe/Braintree/Adyen etc. will return the original result for a repeated request with the same key instead of creating a second charge. This is the piece that makes retrying safe at all.

**2. Track state locally, not just success/failure**
Persist a charge-attempt record with states like `pending → processing → succeeded / failed / timed_out`. On a client-side timeout, set it to `timed_out`, not `failed` — you genuinely don't know the outcome yet. Never show the customer "payment failed" for this state; show "confirming payment" or similar.

**3. Resolve before you retry**
When a timeout happens, the first move isn't "call again," it's "ask what actually happened":
- Query the processor for the status of that idempotency key / payment intent, or
- Just re-send the same idempotent request — the processor will hand back the real outcome instead of double-processing.

Only treat it as retryable if the check comes back "no such charge" / genuinely not started.

**4. Separate retryable from non-retryable failures**
- Retryable: network timeout, connection reset, 5xx/gateway timeout — infrastructure-level, safe to retry.
- Not retryable: card declined, insufficient funds, fraud block — these are real business outcomes; retrying won't help and should surface to the customer immediately as an actual decline, distinct from a timeout.

**5. Backoff and bounded attempts**
Exponential backoff with jitter, capped at a small number of attempts (3–5). Do the first retry or two synchronously if you can stay within a reasonable UX window; beyond that, hand off to a background job so the customer isn't stuck on a spinner.

**6. Durable retry queue / outbox**
For attempts that exhaust synchronous retries, write them to a durable queue (outbox table + worker) so retries survive a process crash or deploy, rather than living only in memory/request scope.

**7. Webhooks as source of truth**
Payment processors often complete the charge asynchronously even if your HTTP call timed out. Subscribe to `charge.succeeded` / `charge.failed`-type webhooks and let them authoritatively update the local charge state — this closes the gap where your retry logic and the processor's actual result disagree.

**8. Tune the timeout itself**
If timeouts are happening "a few times a day," check whether your client timeout is just too aggressive relative to the processor's real p99 latency — sometimes the fix is loosening the timeout + adding async confirmation, rather than more retries.

The one piece that's load-bearing for correctness is #1 — without idempotency keys, every other layer just adds more ways to double-charge someone.

At 38k rows on Postgres 16, Postgres full-text search is the right call — no need for Elasticsearch/Algolia at this scale, and it keeps the stack (Express + `pg`) unchanged.

**Schema**: add a generated `tsvector` column combining name and description, weighted so name matches rank higher, plus a GIN index on it.

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
```

**Query**, ranked by relevance, still filtered to `active`:

```sql
SELECT id, sku, name, price_cents,
       ts_rank(search_vector, query) AS rank
FROM products, plainto_tsquery('english', $1) query
WHERE active AND search_vector @@ query
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 50 OFFSET $2;
```

**Route**: a new `GET /products/search?q=...` (or a `q` param folded into the existing `GET /`), same paging pattern as `routes/products.js` today.

**Typo tolerance**: `to_tsquery`/`plainto_tsquery` won't match "wiht" for "with". If that matters for the roadmap, add `pg_trgm` and a trigram GIN index on `name`, and fall back to a similarity search when the tsquery returns nothing — that's the one real tradeoff: full-text search alone is fast and free but exact-token-based, while trigram/fuzzy adds typo tolerance at the cost of a second index and a slightly messier query.

Revisit this choice (move to a dedicated search service) only if the catalog grows an order of magnitude, or you need faceting/synonyms/relevance tuning beyond what `ts_rank` gives you — not likely at a few hundred rows/month growth.

Given what's already in this repo, the pieces point to one specific design: **direct-to-S3 upload via presigned PUT**, not a multipart upload through the app server. **Why not through the app server:** `nginx.conf:12` caps `client_max_body_size` at 1m for the whole listener (storefront, payments, admin all share it), and the comment says raising it — even per-location — was explicitly declined by the payments team for PCI reasons. Phone camera photos routinely run several MB (a modern JPEG easily hits 3–8MB, more for HEIC), so posting raw photo bytes to `market.example.com` would just hit that 1MB wall. That path is closed, and reopening it means relitigating a PCI decision for an unrelated feature. **What's already built for this:** `storage.js:11-16` supports `signedUrl(key, { method: 'PUT' })`, currently unused, and the bucket's CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com`. `db.js` has `photo_keys` (an empty `text[]`) and `addPhotoKey(id, key)` to append a key. This is the standard shape for bypassing a body-size limit: hand the client a time-limited URL and let it upload straight to S3. **The flow:** 1. Seller's phone calls a new endpoint, e.g. `POST /listings/:id/photos` — through nginx, but this request body is just JSON (filename/content-type), nowhere near 1MB. The handler checks the caller owns listing `:id`, generates a key like `listings/${id}/${uuid}.jpg`, and calls `storage.signedUrl(key, { method: 'PUT' })`. Returns `{ uploadUrl, key }`. 2. The phone `PUT`s the actual photo bytes straight to that S3 URL. This traffic never touches nginx or the app server, so the 1MB limit and the PCI concern behind it are irrelevant here — the app server never sees the bytes. 3. On success, the phone calls a confirm endpoint (small JSON body again) with `{ key }`, which calls `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)` — the exact function already sitting unused in `db.js`. 4. Reading photos back mirrors the existing invoice route (`routes/listings.js:14-17`): for each key in `photo_keys`, call `storage.signedUrl(key)` (default GET) and hand the client a signed URL rather than serving bytes. **Things worth deciding before building it:** - Ownership check on step 1 — nothing in `db.js`/`storage.js` enforces that the caller owns the listing; that has to live in the route handler. - Presigned PUT doesn't itself cap upload size the way a presigned POST with policy conditions can — if an unbounded PUT is a concern, that's the one deviation from the existing PUT-based helper worth considering. - The bucket denies public reads (same policy as the invoice bucket), so listing photos shown on the storefront need refreshed signed GET URLs rather than a plain long-lived `` — same trade-off the invoice link already has, just now on a public-facing page instead of a buyer-only one.

Here's how I'd build it, working from the constraints the spec already lays down (pure `govern()`, supervisor owns all I/O, simulation harness must be able to replay cycles deterministically).

**Split "cap decision" from "alert conditions."**
The guardrail list in `## Guardrails` is priority-ordered and first-match-wins — it picks one guardrail to drive the cap for that cycle. But the `## Observability` list isn't the same list: it includes things like "pinned for two consecutive cycles" and "pace error above 15% for two consecutive cycles," which aren't single-cycle facts, and "heartbeat missed," which isn't a `govern()` output at all. So `result.guardrail` alone can't drive alerting — you'd lose lower-priority conditions any cycle a higher-priority one wins, and you'd have no way to express multi-cycle thresholds.

The fix: extend the persisted controller `state` with small counters (`consecutive_clamped`, `consecutive_pace_error`, plus the `consecutive_stale` the feed_stale fallback already implies), have `govern()` update them each call, and have `govern()` return a second field, `result.alerts` — a list of zero or more alert conditions, evaluated independently of which guardrail won the cap decision. This stays inside the pure core: still just `(state, inputs) -> (cap, state, guardrail, alerts)`, no I/O, so the simulation harness keeps working unchanged and unit tests can assert alert lists directly against a scripted state history.

**Supervisor's job stays mechanical.**
```
result = govern(state, inputs)
apply_cap(tenant, result.cap)
persist_state(tenant, result.state)
for condition in result.alerts:
    alert(condition, tenant)
```
No decision logic here beyond "did govern() tell me to alert."

**Dedup, don't re-page every cycle.**
`quota_exceeded` can hold for hours; a naive `alert()` call fires every five minutes for the whole time. Make `alert()` edge-triggered (or at least give it a stable dedup key like `(tenant, condition)`) and push it through something with built-in grouping/auto-resolve — Alertmanager, PagerDuty dedup keys, Datadog monitors — rather than hand-rolling suppression in the supervisor. The alert event itself carries tenant, condition, cycle timestamp, and the alerting backend's routing decides severity/channel (e.g., one tenant hitting `quota_exceeded` is a ticket, twenty tenants simultaneously is a page — that's a routing rule, not core logic).

**Heartbeat is the odd one out.**
"Supervisor heartbeat missed" can't be produced by code that only runs *when the loop runs* — absence of execution can't emit its own alert. That needs a dead-man's-switch: each successful cycle writes a liveness timestamp (per tenant or fleet-wide), and a separate watchdog — a cron check, or a monitoring platform's built-in "no data" alert — fires independently when that timestamp goes stale. This lives entirely outside `govern()` and outside the per-tenant loop.

**Net shape:** one alerting path sourced from `govern()`'s pure, testable output (`result.alerts`, dedup'd at emission), and one independent watchdog for the loop's own liveness. Everything else — thresholds, consecutive-cycle counting — is just more state threaded through the same pure function the rest of the design already relies on.

This is a small Express + pg service, and it already has a real advantage: every write funnels through one function, `db.write()` in `db.js:13-26`, which opens a transaction, runs one statement, and commits. That single chokepoint is where the audit trail should be anchored — everything else in the design follows from it.

## 1. Row-level diffs live in Postgres triggers, not app code

Route handlers call `db.write()` with hand-built SQL (`routes/accounts.js:7-11`, `routes/orders.js:7-11`, `:15-18`). If the audit log only recorded from inside those handlers, every new route would need someone to remember to log it, and anything that touches the DB outside the app (a migration, a psql session, a future service) would be invisible. A trigger on each audited table is the only thing that can't be forgotten or bypassed by app code:

```sql
CREATE TABLE audit_log (
  id           bigint generated always as identity primary key,
  occurred_at  timestamptz not null default now(),
  table_name   text not null,
  row_pk       text not null,
  action       text not null check (action in ('INSERT','UPDATE','DELETE')),
  actor_id     uuid,               -- from app.user_id, set per-transaction
  request_id   text,               -- from app.request_id, ties to app logs
  old_row      jsonb,
  new_row      jsonb
);
CREATE INDEX ON audit_log (table_name, row_pk);
CREATE INDEX ON audit_log (actor_id);
CREATE INDEX ON audit_log (occurred_at);

CREATE FUNCTION audit_trigger() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO audit_log(table_name, row_pk, action, actor_id, request_id, old_row, new_row)
  VALUES (
    TG_TABLE_NAME,
    coalesce(NEW.id, OLD.id)::text,
    TG_OP,
    nullif(current_setting('app.user_id', true), '')::uuid,
    nullif(current_setting('app.request_id', true), ''),
    CASE WHEN TG_OP <> 'INSERT' THEN to_jsonb(OLD) END,
    CASE WHEN TG_OP <> 'DELETE' THEN to_jsonb(NEW) END
  );
  RETURN coalesce(NEW, OLD);
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER accounts_audit AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON accounts
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_trigger();
CREATE TRIGGER orders_audit AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON orders
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_trigger();
```

One generic function, attached per table. It fires inside the same transaction as the write, so the audit row and the data change commit or roll back together — no window where one succeeds without the other.

## 2. "Who" comes from the session, threaded to the trigger via transaction-local settings

`auth.js:5-13` already resolves every request to `req.user.id`. The gap is getting that identity from the request into the trigger, which only sees table rows, not `req.user`.

The clean way: use Node's `AsyncLocalStorage` to hold the current request's user id and a request id, set once in `sessionUser` (or right after it), and read it inside `db.write()` before the query runs:

```js
// inside db.write(), after BEGIN
await client.query("SELECT set_config('app.user_id', $1, true), set_config('app.request_id', $2, true)",
  [actorId, requestId]);
```

`set_config(..., true)` scopes the setting to the current transaction only (it resets on COMMIT), so it can't leak between pooled connections reused by later requests. This only requires touching `db.write()` — the one chokepoint — not every route.

## 3. Make the audit table tamper-resistant

- The app's DB role gets `INSERT` only on `audit_log`, never `UPDATE`/`DELETE`. Revoke those explicitly.
- No app code path writes to `audit_log` directly — only the trigger does, which runs as the table owner regardless of the calling role's grants (`SECURITY DEFINER`-style behavior is implicit for triggers).
- For compliance-grade tamper evidence, periodically export committed audit rows to append-only, immutable storage (S3 with Object Lock / WORM, or a separate log-shipping target) rather than relying on Postgres permissions alone as the only control.

## 4. Retention

Compliance retention windows (often multi-year) mean this table grows without bound and without deletes. Partition `audit_log` by month (`PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at)`) so old partitions can be detached and archived to cold storage instead of running slow deletes against a live table.

## 5. What this doesn't cover — flag explicitly

- **Reads.** This design is writes only, matching the ask. If compliance later needs "who viewed record X," that's a separate, much higher-volume logging path (typically app/access-log based, not DB-trigger based).
- **Bypassing `db.write()`.** If any future code calls `pool.query()` directly for a write (skipping the transaction wrapper), the trigger still fires and still records the row diff — but `actor_id` would be null since `set_config` never ran. Worth a lint rule or code-review convention that all writes go through `db.write()`.
- **Bulk/admin operations.** Migrations or an admin console hitting the DB with a different role would show up in `audit_log` with `actor_id = null`. Give any such tooling its own service account and have it set `app.user_id` too, so "who" stays meaningful even for non-request-driven writes.
- **Why, not just what.** The trigger captures the row diff, not intent (e.g., "refunded due to customer complaint"). If that's needed, it's a separate application-level event log keyed by the same `request_id`, not a replacement for the row-level trail.

Here's what's in the repo, and it changes the shape of the answer: this isn't a "add a cache" problem, it's a "there's a CDN already sitting in front of everything with a 0% hit rate because of a blanket header policy" problem.

**Root cause of the 0% hit rate**

`middleware/security.js` sets `Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` on every response, applied via `app.use(security)` before both `/p` and `/account`. The comment says it was a blanket fix for an account-page leaking through an intermediary cache, applied app-wide "because that was the fastest way to close the finding" — and never revisited. `/p/:slug` (`routes/products.js`) is fully anonymous: no session read, same price/stock/copy for every visitor. It has no reason to carry `private, no-store`. `/account/orders` genuinely does — that's per-user data and the no-store there is correct.

Since platform engineering won't add path rules at the edge ("policy lives in the app"), the fix has to be in headers: scope the lockdown to `/account`, and let `/p` emit its own `Cache-Control`.

**Layer 1 — CDN (highest leverage, zero DB cost on hit)**

Once `/p` is allowed to set headers, give it something like:

```
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300
```

A hit here never reaches the app or the database — it eliminates the 900ms entirely, not just the DB part. Catalog edits happen "a few times a day" per the route comment, so a TTL of order-of-a-minute is a reasonable default freshness/hit-rate tradeoff. If the admin tool needs faster propagation for something like a price correction, add a purge call (CDN purge API for the specific `/p/:slug` URL) on product save, on top of the TTL as a backstop.

**The wrinkle: stock**

`stockFor` (~250ms) is the most volatile of the three queries — it changes with every purchase, unlike the catalog data. Caching it at the same TTL as the rest of the page means showing possibly-stale stock for up to a minute. Two options:
- **Accept it.** Checkout/cart is a per-user, uncached flow anyway, so actual reservation gets re-validated there — a product page saying "in stock" when the last unit sold 20 seconds ago is a cosmetic staleness, not a correctness bug.
- **Split it out.** Cache the page shell (product + related) at the CDN; fetch stock via a separate small endpoint, client-side, with its own short/no-cache policy. More moving parts — only worth it if stale stock display is an actual business problem, not just a theoretical one.

I'd default to accepting it unless told otherwise.

**Layer 2 — mid-tier cache in front of the DB (protects origin on misses)**

CDN hits don't need this, but every miss — cold start, TTL expiry on a popular slug, a purge, a POP that hasn't cached yet — still pays the full 900ms today. Two problems that layer alone doesn't solve:
- `relatedProducts` (~600ms, the four-table join — the actual bulk of the cost) is worth caching in something like Redis with a short TTL (tens of seconds), independent of the CDN layer, so an edge miss doesn't mean a full DB round-trip.
- Without request coalescing, a hot product's cache expiry causes a thundering herd — N concurrent requests each independently re-running the 600ms join. A single-flight/dedup pattern (in-process or via Redis lock) so concurrent misses for the same slug share one DB query is what actually protects the database under load, more than the cache-hit rate does.

**One thing that isn't caching at all but is sitting right there**

In `routes/products.js`, `relatedProducts(product.id)` and `stockFor(product.id)` are independent of each other once `product.id` is known, but they're awaited sequentially: `40 + 600 + 250 ≈ 890ms`. Running those two concurrently (`Promise.all`) drops it to roughly `40 + max(600, 250) ≈ 640ms` with no caching involved at all. Worth doing regardless of everything else, since it's free.

**Net design**

1. Narrow `security.js`'s `no-store/private` to `/account` only; keep the non-cache-related headers (`X-Frame-Options`, `nosniff`) app-wide.
2. `/p` sets `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300` (tune the numbers), optionally with an admin-triggered purge for the exact slug.
3. Redis (or similar) cache for `relatedProducts`/`productBySlug` in front of the DB, with single-flight on miss, to bound worst-case origin load.
4. Leave `stockFor` live unless staleness turns out to matter, in which case split it into its own lightly-cached endpoint.
5. Parallelize the two independent queries in the route handler as a free win either way.

Two separate problems here: stopping today's bleeding, and building the general system so it doesn't recur.

## Immediate mitigation
Identify the offending client (API key, auth token, or IP from access logs/metrics) and apply a targeted throttle or temporary block at the edge (load balancer, gateway, or WAF) right now. This buys time to build the real thing without new code.

## Rate limiter design

**1. Key by client, not just IP.** Use API key / auth token / tenant ID as the primary identity. Fall back to IP only for unauthenticated traffic — otherwise clients behind NAT or on shared IPs get punished together, and a malicious client can rotate IPs to dodge an IP-based limit.

**2. Algorithm: token bucket.** Give each client a bucket with capacity `C` and refill rate `R` tokens/sec. Each request consumes a token; if the bucket's empty, reject. This allows short bursts (useful for legit clients doing batch work) while capping sustained rate — better UX than a hard fixed-window cap, and simpler to reason about than sliding-window log. Sliding-window counter is a reasonable alternative if you want smoother enforcement without burst allowance.

**3. Enforce at the edge, before the app/DB.** Put it in the gateway/reverse proxy layer (envoy, nginx with a rate-limit module, or a dedicated service like Redis-backed middleware) so rejected requests never reach `/v1`'s backend and consume DB/CPU. This is the key fix for "degrading for everybody" — the problem isn't just that one client is over quota, it's that their traffic is competing for the same shared pool (DB connections, worker threads, etc.) as everyone else.

**4. Shared state via Redis.** If you have multiple app instances, per-instance in-memory counters don't work — a client can spread requests across instances and exceed the real limit. Use Redis with an atomic Lua script (check-and-decrement token count) or `INCR` + `EXPIRE` for the counter approach. This adds a network hop but Redis ops here are sub-millisecond and it's the standard approach (Stripe, GitHub, Cloudflare all do this).

**5. Two tiers of limits, not one:**
   - **Per-client limit** — fair-use cap so no single client can starve others.
   - **Global/backend limit** — a ceiling on total concurrent load into `/v1` regardless of how it's distributed across clients, e.g. via a semaphore or concurrency limiter in front of the backend, or load-shedding when a queue depth/latency SLO is breached. This is what actually protects "everybody else" — per-client limits alone don't help if 500 well-behaved clients collectively exceed capacity.

**6. Response contract.** Return `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header and `X-RateLimit-Limit` / `X-RateLimit-Remaining` / `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers, so well-behaved clients back off automatically instead of retrying immediately and making it worse.

**7. Fairness under contention (optional but relevant to your case).** If you want to avoid outright rejecting a heavy client and instead just prevent them from crowding out others, use weighted fair queuing or priority lanes at the connection-pool level, rather than a binary allow/reject — heavy clients get slower, not blocked.

**8. Observability.** Emit per-client request-rate and reject-rate metrics, and alert on any client crossing e.g. 80% of its limit sustained, so you catch the next noisy neighbor before it degrades the service instead of after.

Typical stack: gateway-level enforcement (envoy/nginx/Kong) + Redis for shared counters + token bucket algorithm + a separate global concurrency cap on the backend. The global cap is the piece most rate-limiter writeups skip, and it's the one that directly answers "degrading for everybody."

Two ways to get rid of manual refresh, in increasing order of complexity:

**1. Polling (simplest, usually sufficient for ops dashboards)**
Frontend re-fetches on an interval (e.g. `setInterval`, or a library feature like React Query's `refetchInterval` / SWR's `refreshInterval`). Backend stays a normal REST endpoint. Add:
- `If-None-Match`/ETag or a `since=<timestamp>` param so unchanged data returns 304/empty instead of a full payload each time.
- Pause polling when the tab is backgrounded (`document.visibilitychange`) to avoid wasted load.
- Stagger requests if many widgets poll independently, or batch them into one endpoint.

This is what most dashboards (Grafana, Datadog, internal admin panels) actually do under the hood, at 5–30s intervals.

**2. Server push (WebSockets or Server-Sent Events)**
Needed if you want sub-second freshness or the data changes are event-driven (alerts firing) rather than time-driven. Pieces:
- Client opens an SSE (`EventSource`) or WebSocket connection instead of polling; UI patches state as messages arrive.
- Backend needs a place to originate the "something changed" signal: Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, Redis pub/sub, Kafka/NATS, etc. Whatever writes the underlying data publishes an event.
- A connection-holding layer (could be the same app server) subscribes to that channel and forwards messages to connected clients.
- If you run multiple server instances, clients on instance A need to hear about changes written via instance B — that's what the pub/sub backbone is for; don't rely on in-process state alone.
- Handle reconnect/backoff on the client and auth on the socket handshake.

**Recommendation:** start with polling — it's a small frontend change, no new infrastructure, and covers "stop making people hit refresh" completely. Move to SSE/WebSockets only if you specifically need near-real-time push (e.g., alerts should appear within a second) or polling load becomes a problem at your dashboard's scale. SSE over WebSockets if the data only flows server→client (typical for a dashboard) — it's simpler to implement and reconnects natively.

Here's the design, grounded in what's already in this repo.

**Why not just POST bytes to the app:** `nginx.conf` caps `client_max_body_size` at 1m globally, shared with the payments listener, and that limit is cited in PCI paperwork — a per-location override for uploads was already declined in March. Phone camera photos routinely run 2–8MB+ (more with HEIC/burst), so routing them through the app server behind this proxy isn't viable without reopening that PCI conversation.

**The intended path is already half-built:** `storage.js` signs PUT as well as GET with the same helper, and its comment notes the bucket CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com`. That's the standard direct-to-S3 pattern, and it sidesteps nginx entirely since the bytes never transit the proxy.

**Flow:**
1. `POST /listings/:id/photos/sign` (small request, fine under the 1MB cap) — app checks the caller owns/can edit listing `:id`, generates a server-side key like `listings/{id}/{uuid}.jpg` (never trust a client-supplied key — avoids path traversal / overwriting other listings), calls `storage.signedUrl(key, { method: 'PUT', expiresIn: 60 })`, returns `{ url, key }`.
2. Client `PUT`s the raw file bytes straight to that S3 URL — no app or nginx involved, no 1MB ceiling, no 30s `proxy_read_timeout` risk on a slow phone upload.
3. `POST /listings/:id/photos` with `{ key }` to confirm — app calls `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)`. Worth a HEAD-on-S3 check here to confirm the object actually landed before trusting the key, since the client's word alone is otherwise the only signal.
4. Repeat 1–3 per photo, or have the sign endpoint accept a count and return several `{url, key}` pairs for multi-select uploads.

**Things this flow doesn't handle for free, worth deciding explicitly:**
- *Size/type enforcement*: a bare presigned PUT doesn't enforce max size or content-type — S3 presigned POST with policy conditions (`content-length-range`, `content-type`) does, if hard limits matter more than client-side checks.
- *HEIC*: iPhones default to HEIC, which most browsers can't render — either force JPEG client-side before upload or transcode server-side after.
- *Serving photos back*: the existing read pattern (`/:id/invoice`) hands out a signed GET URL per request. Fine for one invoice; for a listing page with several photos rendered to any visitor, minting signed URLs per photo per pageview is heavier — a public-read prefix or CDN in front of the bucket is the usual alternative, but that's a separate access-control decision from the upload itself.
- *Post-upload processing* (thumbnails, virus scan): not in this flow at all; would be an S3-event-triggered worker if wanted.

Two places in SPEC.md touch alerting: the pseudocode's `alert("quota exceeded", tenant)` (line 32) and the Observability section's list of eight conditions (lines 64–73). The spec says *what* must alert but not *how* — here's how I'd build it given the constraints the rest of the doc imposes.

**Split the eight conditions by how they're detected, because they don't all fit the same mechanism.**

1. **Single-cycle, straight from `govern()`'s output** — `quota_exceeded`, `floor_at_risk`, `floor_unreachable`, `config_invalid`. These map directly to `result.guardrail`. The supervisor checks `result.guardrail` after each call and fires the matching alert, exactly as the pseudocode already does for `quota_exceeded`. Trivial to extend: a lookup table from guardrail name to alert.

2. **Multi-cycle conditions that need history** — `feed_stale` past three cycles, cap pinned for two consecutive cycles, pace error over 15% for two consecutive cycles. None of these can be read off a single `result`; they need a counter across cycles.
   - The `feed_stale` counter already has to exist somewhere, since `govern()` itself needs it to trigger the 3-cycle fallback to default cap. So that counter is presumably part of the persisted controller state already, and the supervisor can alert off the same counter it's persisting.
   - "Cap pinned at a band edge for two consecutive cycles" and "pace error above 15%" are *not* guardrails in the priority list — `cap_clamped` tells you clamping happened this cycle, but not for how many cycles in a row, and pace error isn't a guardrail at all. Tracking these requires either (a) folding more counters into the pure controller state, which starts pulling alerting concerns into the core the spec is careful to keep I/O-free and simulation-replayable, or (b) keeping a separate, supervisor-owned "alert state" per tenant that isn't touched by `govern()` at all — just a rolling window the supervisor updates after each cycle using `result` and `inputs`. Option (b) fits the architecture better: it keeps `govern()`'s contract (state + inputs → decision) unpolluted by bookkeeping that only alerting needs, and the simulation harness doesn't have to know about it.
   - Pace error itself needs a formula not given in the spec (something like actual processed-so-far vs. expected-pace-given-quota-and-time-of-day) — that's a gap to fill in, either as an extra field `govern()` returns or as something the supervisor computes independently from `inputs`.

3. **Liveness — "Supervisor heartbeat missed"** — this one can't be implemented as code inside the loop, because if the loop isn't running, it can't be the thing that notices. This needs a dead-man's-switch: each successful cycle writes a "last run" timestamp somewhere external (a metrics store, a heartbeat key), and a separate watcher — a monitoring system's dead-man's-switch check, or a plain cron — alerts when that timestamp goes stale past some threshold (e.g. missed two 5-minute cycles). This is a different component from the supervisor entirely.

**A few things the spec doesn't settle that the build would need to:**

- **Firing cadence.** As written, a tenant stuck in `quota_exceeded` would page every single cycle, forever, since the loop re-evaluates every five minutes and the guardrail keeps matching. Real alerting almost always wants edge-triggered firing (alert on transition into the condition, send a resolve when it clears) rather than level-triggered (alert every cycle the condition holds), plus dedup/rate-limiting downstream. That logic lives in the supervisor's alert-sending path, not in `govern()`.
- **Alerting must not block the cycle.** `alert()` should come after `apply_cap`/`persist_state` (which the pseudocode already does) and shouldn't be able to fail the cycle if the paging backend is down — likely fire-and-forget with its own retry/queue, decoupled from the control loop's critical path.
- **Delivery backend** (PagerDuty/Opsgenie/Slack/etc.) is unspecified — `alert()` is presumably a thin wrapper over whatever the org already uses.
- **Scope of "Supervisor heartbeat missed"** — global to the whole job or per-tenant? The control loop iterates all tenants per cycle, so it reads as one process-level liveness check, separate from the seven per-tenant conditions.

This is a clean codebase to hook into — every write already funnels through one chokepoint, and "who" is already resolved before any handler runs. Here's how I'd build the audit trail.

## What you already have going for you

- **`db.js:13-26`** — every write in the service goes through `write()`, which already wraps each call in `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`. This is the one place to instrument, not three.
- **`auth.js:5-13`** — `sessionUser` resolves the session to `req.user` before any route handler runs, on every request. "Who" is already known by the time a write happens; it just isn't threaded into `db.write()` yet (see `accounts.js:7-11`, `orders.js:7-11` — `req.user` is available in scope but never passed down).
- Deletes are soft (`deleted_at`), not `DELETE FROM` — good, since it means row history isn't destroyed at the storage layer even before you add auditing.

## Design: two layers, not one

**Layer 1 — Postgres triggers on each audited table.** This is the enforcement backstop: it captures a write no matter how it happens — through `db.write()`, a future script, a one-off `psql` session, a migration. Application-level logging alone can always be bypassed by something that skips the app.

**Layer 2 — actor context injected per-transaction.** Triggers can see the row change but not *who* made it — Postgres has no concept of your app's users. So `db.write()` sets a session variable at the start of its transaction, and the trigger reads it.

```sql
-- inside db.write(), before the real query, still within BEGIN/COMMIT:
SET LOCAL app.user_id = '$1';
SET LOCAL app.user_email = '$2';
SET LOCAL app.request_id = '$3';
```

`SET LOCAL` scopes the variable to the current transaction, so it can't leak across pooled connections — important since `db.js` uses a `Pool`.

## Propagating the actor without touching every route

Rather than editing every call site in `accounts.js`/`orders.js` to pass `req.user` into `write()`, use Node's `AsyncLocalStorage`, populated once in `sessionUser`:

- `auth.js` middleware sets `als.run({ userId, email, requestId }, next)` after resolving `req.user`.
- `db.write()` reads from the ALS store and issues the `SET LOCAL` statements before the caller's query, inside the same transaction it already opens.

This means the two-line change in `auth.js` and `db.js` covers every current and future call to `db.write()` automatically — no per-route edits, no risk of a new route forgetting to pass actor context.

## The audit table

```sql
CREATE TABLE audit_log (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  occurred_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  table_name    text NOT NULL,
  row_pk        text NOT NULL,
  operation     text NOT NULL CHECK (operation IN ('INSERT','UPDATE','DELETE')),
  actor_user_id uuid,
  actor_email   text,           -- denormalized: survives the user later being deleted
  account_id    uuid,           -- tenant, for scoped compliance queries
  request_id    text,           -- correlates multiple row changes to one API call
  old_row       jsonb,
  new_row       jsonb,
  changed_cols  text[]
);
```

Generic trigger function, attached to `accounts`, `orders`, and any other compliance-relevant table:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION audit_row() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO audit_log (table_name, row_pk, operation, actor_user_id, actor_email,
                          request_id, old_row, new_row, changed_cols)
  VALUES (
    TG_TABLE_NAME,
    COALESCE(NEW.id, OLD.id)::text,
    TG_OP,
    nullif(current_setting('app.user_id', true), '')::uuid,
    nullif(current_setting('app.user_email', true), ''),
    nullif(current_setting('app.request_id', true), ''),
    CASE WHEN TG_OP <> 'INSERT' THEN to_jsonb(OLD) END,
    CASE WHEN TG_OP <> 'DELETE' THEN to_jsonb(NEW) END,
    CASE WHEN TG_OP = 'UPDATE'
      THEN (SELECT array_agg(key) FROM jsonb_each(to_jsonb(NEW))
            WHERE to_jsonb(NEW)->key IS DISTINCT FROM to_jsonb(OLD)->key)
    END
  );
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER accounts_audit AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON accounts
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_row();
CREATE TRIGGER orders_audit AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON orders
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_row();
```

`current_setting(..., true)` returns null instead of erroring when unset — covers migrations or console access where no actor context exists, and those rows show up with `actor_user_id = NULL`, which is itself useful (flags writes that bypassed the app entirely).

## Making it tamper-resistant

- `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON audit_log FROM app_role;` — the application's own DB role can insert but never modify or erase history. Even a compromised app can't cover its tracks.
- Trigger function runs as its owner (`SECURITY DEFINER` or just owned by a migration role, not `app_role`), so app-level SQL injection can't disable it.
- For stronger integrity guarantees (some compliance regimes want this), add a `prev_hash`/`row_hash` column, hash-chained like a ledger, and periodically export to WORM storage (S3 Object Lock, etc.).

## Guardrail against drift

Add a CI check (or a migration-review step) that fails if a new table is created without a matching audit trigger — otherwise this quietly rots the first time someone adds a table and forgets. A quick query against `information_schema.triggers` vs. `information_schema.tables` catches it.

## Net effect

- "Who" — `actor_user_id`/`actor_email`, sourced from the session middleware that already runs on every request, propagated via `AsyncLocalStorage` + `SET LOCAL`, no per-route changes needed.
- "What" — full before/after row state and changed-column list, captured by triggers so no write path can skip it.
- "When" — `occurred_at`, server-side, not client-supplied.
- Bonus: `request_id` lets you reconstruct "this one API call touched these N rows" for incident review.
